etymology: English: the sentence at the end of an advertisement that names who paid for it - in the United States, "I'm a candidate and I approve this message."
effect: Puts the funder's name inside the advertisement, in the same medium and before the vote, at the size of the claim rather than the size of the footnote.
costs: A disclosure rule enforced against bodies that can afford better lawyers than the regulator can.
failure: The disclaimer read at speed over the last half-second, and the shell company whose name is a noun with an LLC after it.
tell: A funder named in the ad, not after it
A list published before the ballot
A shell company that has to name its own shell

confused_with.tell: The records request produces the document after the decision; the sponsor line puts the payer's name in front of the audience before the vote.

senses: The disclosure requirement attached to political spending: whoever pays for the advertisement is named inside it, at the same moment and in the same medium as the claim.

It works because anonymity is the doctrine's operating condition - an argument made by a body nobody can summon is an argument nobody can answer. The sponsor line does not cap the spending; it makes the spender answerable to the audience the spending was aimed at.
example: *"**The sponsor line** ran for four seconds under a ninety-second advertisement, and the four seconds were the only part of it anybody could check."*
